snip.t: Early oral or enteral feeding is encouraged (enhanced recovery).
snip.s: Post-operative Care and Complications of Surgery

snip.t: Enteral feeding is best because it is more physiological, has fewer complications, preserves the gut mucosa (prevents villous atrophy and bacterial translocation), and is cheaper than parenteral feeding.
snip.s: Nutritional Support in Surgical Patients: Enteral Feeding and TPN

snip.t: Early feeding: oral intake as tolerated within 24 to 48 hours; nasojejunal or enteral feeding if severe.
snip.s: Internal Medicine CAT 1 (MBIM 6112), 2019/2020: gastroenterology and hepatology,

snip.t: Contra‑indications: avoid routine prophylactic antibiotics, avoid early aggressive enteral feeding in patients with ileus, avoid NSAIDs in renal failure or active GI bleed.
Start low‑calorie enteral feeding (≈10 kcal/kg/day) and increase by 10–20 % daily.
Begin low‑calorie enteral feeding with thiamine supplementation
| Feeding access | PEG (percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy) for prolonged enteral feeding (neurological dysphagia, head and neck cancer) |

snip.t: Enteral feeding, particularly with formula (hyperosmolar feeds, rapid advancement) provides substrate for bacterial fermentation.

qs.q: What is the recommended bed elevation angle for the prevention of hospital-acquired pneumonia in patients receiving oral or enteral feeding?
o: 30 to 45 degrees elevation of the bed
0 to 15 degrees elevation of the bed
15 to 30 degrees elevation of the bed
60 to 75 degrees elevation of the bed
qs.e: Elevation of the head of the bed to 30-45 degrees helps prevent aspiration and subsequent hospital-acquired pneumonia. Flat positioning increases reflux risk.
